text: The book states the Dirichlet function (f(x) = 1 for x ∈ ℚ, f(x) = 0 for x ∉ ℚ) is not Riemann integrable on [0, 1]. What reason does it give?
choices: It has only finitely many discontinuities.
On every subinterval inf f = 0 and sup f = 1, so every lower sum is 0 and every upper sum is 1, and sup L(f,P) ≠ inf U(f,P).
Its Riemann sums depend on the mesh but not on the choice of sample points.
explanation: By the Darboux criterion the function is integrable iff sup L(f,P) = inf U(f,P). Every subinterval contains both rationals and irrationals, so L(f,P) = 0 and U(f,P) = 1 for all partitions P, and these never agree. The function is bounded, so option 0 is false; it is discontinuous everywhere rather than finitely often, so option 1 (which would actually imply integrability) is wrong; and its sums do depend on sample-point choice, so option 3 is backwards.
